scenes.text: Every engineer has used an AI coding assistant. And every engineer has watched one lose track of the file that matters, rewrite a function nobody asked it to touch, or confidently edit a symbol that doesn't exist. We built the coding agent we actually wanted to use.

The problem isn't only quality. It's trust. In the last year, real vulnerabilities in Copilot, Cursor, Cline and Roo Code let hidden instructions in a repository turn on auto-approval, run arbitrary commands, and leak secrets. An agent that can write to your machine has to be built for that world from day one.

This is Anvil, an editor-native coding agent for VS Code. It does four things exceptionally well. It finds the right code, even in a repository bigger than any context window. It never changes a file without showing you the diff, hunk by hunk. It keeps working when a model fails. And it's secure by design.

Under the hood, Anvil runs its agent loop on TrueForge, TrueFoundry's open-source agent harness. The extension is a client of a TrueForge agent. Every editor capability, from retrieval and search to reviewed writes and approved commands, is exposed as an MCP tool. So the agent decides what to read and what to change, and TrueForge's approval gate drives every diff review. Your model lives in TrueForge, never in the extension. Bring Gemini, Groq, or a local model through Ollama.

Context is where agents win or lose. Anvil indexes the repository at the level of functions, classes and documentation sections, ranks them with BM25, and then does something most tools don't. It pulls in the counterparts a real change needs: the test file, and the docs page. All of it under a strict token budget, with the reason for every choice shown to you.

scenes.caption: Inline edit · live
scenes.text: Let's see it live, on the Flask repository. Select a function, press Control Alt K, and describe the change in plain English. The diff streams straight into the editor, and you accept or reject each hunk. Run the check: with FLASK DEBUG set to off, it now prints False. And any applied change is one click away from being reverted.

scenes.caption: Agent mode · multi-file · live
scenes.text: Now the hard one. A single request: add a flask config command that masks secrets, register it, test it, and document it. No files named. Anvil assembles the context, and the agent explores the codebase on its own. Every edit arrives as a reviewable diff. Watch the reviewer reject a change to unrelated test infrastructure, and keep what was asked for. The tests pass, and the new command prints the configuration, with every secret masked.

scenes.caption: Resilience · live
scenes.text: Models fail. Endpoints go down, keys expire, quotas run out. Here the primary model is unreachable. Anvil retries with backoff, then fails over to the next model automatically, and the edit still lands. With no fallback left, you get a clear error, the editor never freezes, and git status stays clean.

We hardened Anvil against everything we hit in real runs. It honours a provider's rate-limit hints and resumes the same session, so no progress is lost. A daily quota triggers an immediate fallback. If a model writes a tool call as plain text, or stops after exploring without making the change, Anvil notices and steers it back. And a circuit breaker stops runaway loops before they burn your budget.

Security was designed in, not bolted on. We studied the published attacks on AI coding tools and grouped them into thirteen classes. Config files that could grant code execution need explicit confirmation. Secrets never reach the model. Hidden Unicode is exposed. Risky commands are rated and need a deliberate decision. Our local server rejects DNS rebinding and cross-site requests. And every action lands in an audit log.

scenes.caption: Security · live
scenes.text: Here, a prompt-injected edit tries to switch on auto-approval in VS Code settings and leak data through a remote schema. Anvil flags both before anything touches disk. Then the attack simulation tests run, live.

Every claim in this video is backed by a test. Forty unit tests, including attack simulations over real HTTP. Ten integration tests inside a real VS Code. And the three demo tasks, verified live against TrueForge with real models.
Anvil. Context you can see. Changes you control. An agent that keeps working when models fail. Built on TrueForge.
